arguments.value: iBio and Beijing CC-Pharming entered into a master agreement to work together on multiple biopharmaceutical development projects, with each project covered by a separate statement of work. iBio gives CC-Pharming a limited, nonexclusive license to use iBio’s plant-based protein technology only to develop, manufacture, and seek regulatory approval for products in China, and not for export or use elsewhere. The first project is a plant-made rituximab product, and iBio will provide technology transfer, development support, facility design consulting, training, and regulatory and quality-system assistance. CC-Pharming must pay iBio milestone-based fees tied to project deliverables. The agreement says that inventions and copyrights created individually belong to the creator, while joint creations are jointly owned, with patent costs shared equally. Both sides must keep confidential information secret for five years, can negotiate commercial licenses to new inventions or copyrighted materials, and can publish only within the agreement’s confidentiality limits. The contract includes standard terms on no warranties, limited liability, dispute escalation, force majeure, export controls, assignment restrictions, Texas law and Texas/U.S. federal courts, and termination for material breach after notice and cure period.
